headline: A PKCS #11 URI names a token and an object on it, read and written to the RFC 7512 grammar.
summary: An operator pointing a tool at a key in a hardware security module, a smart card or a PIV slot names it with an RFC 7512 URI rather than a file path, and every PKCS #11 consumer from OpenSSL to p11-kit reads that syntax. The toolkit had no way to read or write one. `pki.pkcs11.parseUri` and `pki.pkcs11.formatUri` are that syntax and nothing more: nothing here loads a module or talks to a token.

Added: `pki.pkcs11.parseUri(uri)` reads an RFC 7512 PKCS #11 URI into `{ path, vendorPath, query, vendorQuery }`. The path carries what identifies the object (`token`, `manufacturer`, `serial`, `model`, the three `library-*` attributes, the three `slot-*` attributes, `object`, `type` and `id`) and the query what tells a consumer how to reach it (`pin-source`, `pin-value`, `module-name`, `module-path`). A vendor attribute in either component is kept under its own name. A vendor query attribute carries a list of its values, which sec. 2.4 permits to repeat and leaves to the consumer to interpret; a vendor path attribute carries one value, sec. 2.3 admitting no repeat. Each record is prototype-less, so a computed read answers from the URI and never from `Object.prototype`. `id` is a `Buffer`, because the attribute names bytes rather than text, and `slot-id` and `library-version` are read as numbers.

`pki.pkcs11.formatUri(record)` writes the record back in canonical form: attributes in the order the RFC lists them, vendor attributes sorted, each value percent-encoded to what its own component admits unencoded, `id` encoded whole with uppercase hexadecimal, `slot-id` without leading zeros and `library-version` stating its minor. That is what lets two URIs naming one object be compared as strings, which sec. 2.6 asks of a consumer, and the form is stable: writing it again changes nothing. One difference it keeps is the order of a repeated vendor query attribute's values, since sec. 2.4 leaves what a repeat means to the consumer and the order may carry part of it. An attribute name and a `type` value are read whichever case they arrive in, RFC 5234 sec. 2.3 making an ABNF quoted literal case-insensitive, and carried in one spelling; so `PIN-SOURCE` is the `pin-source` attribute and is held to the rules `pin-source` is held to, rather than passing as vendor data. The fold is the ASCII one the grammar is written in, not the Unicode one, so a name carrying a character that Unicode folds onto an ASCII letter, such as the Kelvin sign onto `k`, is refused rather than read as the attribute it resembles.
Changed: A builder that encodes text now requires text. `pki.asn1.build.utf8`, `.ia5`, `.printable` and `.bmpString` refuse a value that is not a string with `asn1/bad-string`, `pki.cbor.build.textString` refuses one with `cbor/bad-argument`, and a `pki.pkcs12.build` bag whose `friendlyName` is not a string is refused with `pkcs12/bad-input`. Each of those used to turn the value into text first, so an object was encoded as `[object Object]` and a list as its members joined with a comma, and the certificate, message or key store carried that instead of anything the caller named. Pass the string; where the value came from bytes, decode it yourself and pass the result.

`pki.asn1.encode` takes bytes for its content: a `Buffer`, a typed array, a list of byte values, or nothing for an empty value. A string, an object, a number, and a list carrying an element outside 0 to 255 are refused with `asn1/not-buffer`. Each of those used to be converted, so a string became its UTF-8 encoding, an object went through its `valueOf`, an element past 255 became that element modulo 256, and a number ended the call with a Node argument fault rather than a `PkiError`.
Security: Parsing follows the sec. 2.3 and sec. 2.4 grammar rather than a general URI reader, and refuses with its own `pkcs11/*` code rather than guessing: a character the component admits only percent-encoded, a truncated or non-hexadecimal escape, a value that is not valid UTF-8, an empty attribute between two delimiters, an attribute that appears twice where the RFC admits it once, a percent-escape inside `type`, `slot-id` or `library-version`, whose grammar is literal alternatives and digit runs, a `type` outside the five the RFC enumerates, a `library-version` component above 255, each being one byte in the `CK_INFO` structure sec. 2.3 points at, a URI carrying both `pin-source` and `pin-value`, and a `module-path` that is not absolute on any platform this toolkit runs on. The last two are what sec. 2.4 asks a consumer to treat as invalid: one leaves which PIN applies undecided, and the other decides which shared object a process loads from wherever it happens to be running.

Writing is held to the same rules, so the formatter never emits a URI the parser would refuse. A vendor attribute name is held to the vendor grammar and refused when a standard attribute owns it, which is what keeps a name carrying a delimiter from putting an attribute into the URI that the caller never named and that the standard attribute's own checks never saw. A vendor name given no value, or given an empty list, is refused rather than dropped, so the URI that comes back carries every attribute that was asked for or the call fails. Every component of the record is read once, before anything is written, and a text attribute must be given a string rather than a value turned into one, so nothing a caller passes can run code partway through a write and add an attribute to a component whose checks have already passed.
